.PHONY: test test-fast

test-fast:
	python -m pytest -m "not postgres and not integration" -q

test:
	python -m pytest -q
# ledgerline

Ledgerline is the invoicing and billing servce for Acme. It creates invoices,
computes tax, posts finalized invoices to the external ledger, and exports
monthly reports.

## Layout

- `src/billing/` - money, invoices, refunds, and tax logic
- `src/api/` - the HTTP endpoints
- `migrations/` - the SQL schema migrations
- `scripts/` - operational scripts

## Development

Install the dependancies with `pip install -e .[dev]`, then run the tests.
export.py

You cut a release by pushing a git tag in the form `vYYYY.MM.N`. CI then builds and publishes it. Don't publish by hand.

```bash
git checkout main && git pull
git tag v2026.10.1     # year.month.N, where N is the release number within that month
git push origin v2026.10.1
```

For example, `v2026.09.2` was the second release of September 2026. If this is the first release of October, the tag would be `v2026.10.1`.

This comes from a project memory written by a person, not from anything in the repo. I couldn't confirm it from this checkout:
- There's no CI config in the repo (no `.github/workflows` or anything similar), so I can't see what the tag push triggers. The pipeline probably lives somewhere else.
- The local clone has no tags at all, so I couldn't check the numbering against past releases. Run `git fetch --tags` first to see the latest tag and choose the next `N`.
- The README and Makefile don't describe a release process. The Makefile only has `test` and `test-fast` targets.

It's a good idea to run `make test` on `main` before tagging. If you can tell me where the CI pipeline is defined, I can check what it actually does when a tag is pushed.
